items.title: AI engineering
items.body: I'm interested in enterprise RAG, AI agents, and workflows. I care more about the work they can save someone than how many models they connect to.

items.title: Full-stack products
items.body: I build web and desktop apps. Alongside APIs and data, I pay attention to how a page reads and whether an interaction feels awkward.

items.title: Forward deployed engineering
items.body: FDE interests me because there's plenty to ask before writing code: who will use it, how, and which systems it needs to connect to. Deployment and maintenance are worth spending time learning, too.

items.title: Agree on the change first
items.body: I ask AI to read the existing code and explain what it plans to change. If we understand the task differently, I'd rather discuss that before it's halfway through.

items.title: Keep asking until I understand
items.body: I don't stop at a reviewer's conclusion. I ask what the issue affects and what happens if I leave it alone, then decide whether to make the change.

items.title: Keep the scope in check
items.body: I finish the change I set out to make. If the model suggests a refactor or a new feature along the way, I consider it separately instead of accepting it by default.

items.title: Revise the rules as I go
items.body: When the same mistake keeps happening, I add a project rule for it. My configuration changes with experience; it doesn't need to cover everything on day one.

About.title: I'm
About.intro: I'm Dingxin Tao, an AI Native developer. I studied Computer Science at Shoreline Community College and UC Irvine, and am now studying Analytics at USC.

paragraphs: AI lets me try more of the things I want to make. I use it to write code, review changes, and think things through. It also helped build this website and the projects here.

I don't treat a model's answer as a decision. If I don't understand a review comment, I ask what it affects. If a suggestion doesn't fit what I'm trying to do, I stop and talk it through. I still have to decide what to change.

I have my own taste in interfaces. Oversized type, a hitch in an animation, or a cropped screenshot will make me want to go back and fix it. I'm the same with copy: if it doesn't sound like something I'd say, I change it.

Some projects here are independent work; others build on open source. Omnigate, for example, is based on new-api. I separate what the upstream project provides from what I changed. My blog describes how I work right now. Some of it may only suit me, and you're free to disagree.

Writing down how I use and configure AI coding tools.

items.title: Make my own calls
items.body: A model can suggest changes, and I can switch tools. I want to understand the reasoning before I adopt a suggestion.

items.title: My setup isn't a standard
items.body: What works for me may not fit another project. I can explain my choices without expecting everyone to agree.

items.title: Be clear about sources
items.body: When I use an open-source project, I explain what it provides. If AI helped, I say so.

items.title: Follow my own taste
items.body: I don't like introductions packed with jargon. I prefer simple pages and writing that feels natural to read.
